response.answer_text: The light-dependent reactions convert light energy into chemical energy stored in energy carriers, and these carriers transport that energy to the Calvin cycle. The light-dependent reactions use light to temporarily store energy in energy carriers [ev_005] [ev_008]. Photosystems absorb light and use electron transport chains to convert energy into the chemical energy of ATP and NADPH [ev_002]. These energy-carrying molecules travel into the stroma, where the Calvin cycle reactions take place [ev_007]. The Calvin cycle then uses the energy in ATP and NADPH to convert CO2-derived molecules into G3P [ev_010]. The carriers are described as "full" when they carry energy from the light-dependent reactions, and they return as "empty" carriers to the light-dependent reactions to obtain more energy after the energy is released [ev_001] [ev_005]. The Calvin cycle is the set of reactions that use the energy stored by the light-dependent reactions to form glucose and other carbohydrate molecules [ev_011].
